El <em>Data Encryption Standard</em> es: The Data Encryption Standard is a 16-round Feistel network over 64-bit blocks, with a 56-bit key. Its function $f$ expands the right half's 32 bits to 48, mixes them with 48 bits of the round key, passes them through eight S-boxes from 6 bits to 4 and permutes the result. It was published in full detail, examined for decades, and nobody found a practical shortcut: differential cryptanalysis needs $2^{47}$ chosen texts, and linear cryptanalysis $2^{43}$ known ones. Its only defect was the one visible from the first day: 56 bits are $7\cdot 10^{16}$ keys, and machines kept getting faster.

La [[cr-bloque|red de sustitución y perm: The [[cr-bloque|substitution-permutation network]] needs every step to have an inverse, and designing invertible S-boxes is a constraint. This topic presents a structure that undoes itself even though its inner function has no inverse, using [[cr-vernam|XOR's property]] of cancelling itself. With it the cipher that protected the world for twenty years was built, and with it you can see why it stopped being good enough.
